citation.title: Editorial Bias in Crowd-Sourced Political Information

standing_assumptions:
The article (PLOS ONE 10(9): e0136327, published September 2, 2015; eight pages, printed page n/8 = PDF page n) is an empirical report of randomized field experiments on Wikipedia. It has no theorem, proposition, lemma or proof, no displayed formula and no formal notation; its quantitative statements are in running text, in Fig 1 and in the tables of the twelve Supporting Information files S1–S12. The supplements are DOCX files with no fixed pagination: ‘rendered p.’ below is the page of the validators' renderings of those files, saved under the artifact folders that the targets name. Everything quoted below was read from page images: the main article from staged/pages/p-N.png, the supplements from those renderings.
(S1) Studies and populations. p. 2/8–3/8 (PDF pp. 2–3): “During the summer and fall of 2014, we conducted four studies on Wikipedia, all of which followed the same basic design. Studies 1, 2, and 4 were conducted on the English-language Wikipedia pages of the 100 current U.S. senators, while Study 3 was conducted on the 151 English-language Wikipedia pages of senators who have passed away or otherwise left the Senate since 1990 and do not currently hold any elective office or serve as a Cabinet Secretary.”
(S2) Treatments. p. 3/8 (PDF p. 3): “In each study, research assistants collected one true positive and one true negative fact from a reputable news source on each senator that was not currently mentioned on that senator’s Wikipedia page. [...] For each study, we then randomly assigned half of the pages to have a positive fact added to the page and the other half to have a negative fact added to the page.” “In Studies 1 and 4, we used a factorial design, where we also randomized half of the pages to include a citation with the fact, and the other half without a citation. In Studies 2 and 3, we always included a citation. S1–S4 Files present randomization checks and report the expected covariate balance across the treatment conditions for each study. In S5 File, we report one concluding study to replicate Studies 1 and 4 that was partially aborted due to problems in the implementation, the inclusion of which does not change the results.”
(S3) Implementation. p. 3/8 (PDF p. 3), ‘Implementation on Wikipedia’: “After the facts were collected and senators were randomly assigned to experimental conditions, we inserted the facts into the corresponding senator’s Wikipedia article in the section that seemed most appropriate. In order to prevent confounding, the order in which the edits were made, the time of day, the name of the editing Wikipedia account, and the IP address used to make the edit were randomly assigned as well. With the exception of Study 1, new accounts were created before each study began and were seeded with true, cited, political, non-Senate edits to Wikipedia. More details are presented in S1–S4 Files.” S1 File (rendered p. 1), ‘Details of Random Assignment’: “Senators were first randomly assigned into 25 blocks of 4. Within each block, 2 senators were randomly assigned to receive a negative fact and 2 were randomly assigned to receive a positive fact. Independent of the type of fact, 2 senators were randomly assigned to have the fact cited and 2 senators were randomly assigned to have the fact uncited. The date, time, and account used to make the edits were randomly assigned as well .”
(S4) Outcome and model. p. 4/8 (PDF p. 4), ‘Estimation of Experimental Effects’: “Our primary dependent variable is the survival time of the facts–the amount of time between when the fact is added to Wikipedia and when it is removed. To assess the statistical difference in the survival times between the experimental conditions, we use a Cox proportional hazard model [32].” p. 4/8, Results: “Pooling across studies, negative facts are far more likely to be removed than positive facts by other Wikipedia editors (hazard ratio = 1.59, a measure of the rate at which an event happens in one treatment group over another, p = 0.001).”
(S5) Conventions of the supplementary tables. In the Cox tables of the supplements each entry stands under ‘Coefficient:’ with a parenthesized entry under ‘Standard error:’ beneath it (S6, S9 and S10 were read for this list; finding P041-N013 records the same heading in S7 and S8), and the tables of S6, S9 and S11 used below each carry a note of the form “*Significant at the 10% level; **Significant at the 5% level; ***Significant at the 1% level; Fixed Effects refer to fixed effects for study wave; Covariates Yes means controlling for the date and time order in which an edit was randomly assigned to be made, a binary variable for Republicans, Senate class, region (NE, S, W), length of incumbency, log of Wikipedia page character count before Study 1 began, log of state population, and a dichotomous influence variable for party leaders and committee chairs.” (S10's note stops after “Fixed Effects refer to fixed effects for study wave”. The note of S6 Table E has in addition, after the legend of the stars, “^Date of entry, and hour of entry removed to avoid convergence issues;”, the caret being attached to ‘Yes^’ in the Covariates row of the column ‘5 (1st Half)’.) The entries headed ‘Coefficient:’ in the Cox tables are hazard ratios (exponentiated Cox coefficients) for positive against negative facts and for cited against uncited facts, with standard errors on the hazard-ratio scale: S6 Table A (‘Pooled Cox Regression Estimates’, rendered p. 1) prints Positive 0.629*** (0.091), N 300, and Cited 0.429*** (0.069), N 200, and the main text's 1.59 and 2.33 are their reciprocals (finding P041-N013, rated a clarity note). The paper does not say how the stars are computed.
(S6) Not in the paper: the deposited data. The replication archive (Harvard Dataverse doi:10.7910/DVN/WT4I9N, V1.0; staged/code/harvard-dataverse-WT4I9N-v1.0/) has 551 rows: 100 for each of Studies 1, 2, 4 and 5 and 151 for Study 3. Its codebook codes treatment 1 as positive and cited, 2 as positive and uncited, 3 as negative and cited, 4 as negative and uncited. Studies 1, 2 and 4 each have 50 positive and 50 negative facts; Studies 1 and 4 each have 50 cited and 50 uncited facts; Study 3 has 75 positive and 76 negative facts. Following the deposited do-file (lines 11–15), a fact counts as removed by a horizon of $h$ hours when it has a recorded removal and its stored duration in milliseconds, multiplied by $2.77778\times10^{-7}$, is at most $h$; a fact with no recorded removal survives every horizon used here. The counts used in the targets (removals by 4, 6, 12, 24, 72 and 168 hours, by study and arm) were recounted from the staged CSV when this list was fixed and agree with the validators' artifacts.
(S7) Rounding. A number printed with three decimals as $v$ stands for a value in $[v - 0.0005,\ v + 0.0005]$; a whole-number percentage $k$ is the rounding of $x$ when $k - \tfrac12 \le x < k + \tfrac12$. No quantity used below lies at a rounding tie.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: ‘Replication on Wikipedia Pages of Dead and Retired Senators’, last two sentences (‘This suggests that the editorial bias cannot be explained by … Instead, our findings suggest the editorial bias is limited to active politicians’), and Discussion, first paragraph (‘suggesting that this bias is limited to the pages of active politicians and is not systemic to Wikipedia’): the inference from the Study 3 comparison to confinement of the bias; the witness is the validator's construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 5/8 (PDF p. 5); the claim recurs in the Abstract, p. 1/8 (PDF p. 1)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact countermodel (validator's construction; not in the paper): two populations with the same non-null relative bias and very different absolute contrasts.
Setting. For $q \in (0,1)$ let positive facts be removed at the constant hazard $\lambda_+(q) = -2\log(q)/12$ and negative facts at the constant hazard $\lambda_-(q) = -3\log(q)/12$ (time in hours), so that the survival functions are $S_\pm(t;q) = \exp(-\lambda_\pm(q)\,t)$; equivalently $S_+(t;q) = q^{t/6}$ and $S_-(t;q) = q^{t/4}$. Write $D(q) = S_+(12;q) - S_-(12;q)$ for the positive-minus-negative difference in the probability of surviving 12 hours. Population A (‘active’) has $q_A = 4/5$; population F (‘former’) has $q_F = 99/100$.
Claims. (i) For every $q \in (0,1)$: $\lambda_+(q) > 0$, $\lambda_-(q) > 0$ and $\lambda_+(q)/\lambda_-(q) = 2/3$. So in both populations the hazards are proportional at every time, with the same positive-to-negative hazard ratio $2/3 \ne 1$ (negative-to-positive: $3/2$). (ii) For every $q \in (0,1)$: $S_+(12;q) = q^2$, $S_-(12;q) = q^3$ and $D(q) = q^2(1-q)$. (iii) In A: $S_+(12) = 16/25$, $S_-(12) = 64/125$ and $D(q_A) = 16/125 = 0.128$. In F: $S_+(12) = 9801/10000$, $S_-(12) = 970299/1000000$ and $D(q_F) = 9801/1000000 = 0.009801$. (iv) $D(q_A) - D(q_F) = 118199/1000000 > 0$ and $D(q_A)/D(q_F) = 128000/9801 > 13$. (v) The probabilities of removal within 12 hours are $1 - S_-(12) = 61/125$ and $1 - S_+(12) = 9/25$ in A, and $29701/1000000$ and $199/10000$ in F. Each lies strictly between 0 and 1, so with independent facts each of the four observed 12-hour removal counts (75 of 150 negative and 52 of 150 positive facts in Studies 1, 2, 4; 1 of 76 negative and 3 of 75 positive facts in Study 3) has positive probability $\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$ under the model.
Consequence. The positive-to-negative hazard ratio is $2/3$ in F exactly as in A, although the absolute 12-hour contrast in F is less than one thirteenth of that in A. Hence a smaller, or undetected, absolute contrast on former senators' pages does not imply that the relative bias is absent there or ‘limited to’ population A, and a difference in absolute contrasts between the two populations does not exclude a common editorial preference.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. Survival time, the Cox proportional hazard model and the hazard ratio: standing assumption (S4). Positive and negative facts: (S2). The two populations (the 100 current senators of Studies 1, 2, 4; the 151 former senators of Study 3): (S1). The Study 3 result on which the inference rests, p. 5/8: “Both among senators who have left office and are still living and those who have passed away, we find no differences in the rates in which positive and negative facts are removed ($p$ = 0.70 and 0.47, respectively and $p$ = 0.42, pooled).” S6 Table C (‘Study 3 Cox Regression Estimates for Dead and Retired Senators’, rendered p. 2): Positive, Coefficient 0.691 | 0.775 | 0.627, Standard error (0.318) | (0.503) | (0.406), N 151 | 72 | 79, Studies 3 | 3 (Retired) | 3 (Dead). S6 Table A (rendered p. 1): Positive 0.629*** (0.091), N 300. The inference itself is transcribed in P041-T11.
From the deposited data (S6): the four 12-hour removal counts in (v).
Not in the paper and defined by the validator (P041-E006/v1/artifact/derivation.md, section 6): the exponential removal laws, the parameter $q$ (the 12-hour survival probability is $q^2$ for positive and $q^3$ for negative facts), and $D$. ‘Relative bias’ is a positive-to-negative hazard ratio different from 1, the quantity the paper's Cox models estimate; ‘absolute contrast’ is a difference between the two arms in the probability of surviving a fixed horizon, the quantity the OLS tables of S11 estimate.
canonical_claim.note: A counterexample to an implication, not a model fitted to the paper's data. It does not show that the relative bias on former senators' pages is non-zero; Sol's verdict is confirmed in part (‘An inferential overstatement, narrower than a demonstration that the population claim is false’). What a proof establishes: the pattern the paper reports, a clear contrast on active senators' pages and a small, undetected one on former senators' pages, arises under a law in which the relative bias is identical in the two populations, so the pattern does not entail confinement to active politicians. Part (v) is the validator's check that the model does not contradict the observed counts; positivity is immediate. The validator also reports the joint probability of the four counts (about 0.000118) and its ratio to the product of the four binomial maxima (about 0.314), with the exact rationals in P041-E006/v1/artifact/exact_values.json; these two numbers are not part of the target (‘This ratio is not a p-value or a goodness-of-fit assessment of the full survival data’). The script is P041-E006/v1/artifact/exact_check.py with output exact_output.txt. All fractions above were recomputed in exact arithmetic when this list was fixed. The second validator (v2) confirmed the finding by recalculation from the source and adds no further construction.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: ‘Replication on Wikipedia Pages of Dead and Retired Senators’, last two sentences, and Discussion, first paragraph, last sentence, as repaired by Sol: nondetection in Study 3 with an imprecise relative estimate, smaller early absolute contrasts, and no exclusion of a relative bias on former senators' pages
canonical_claim.location: p. 5/8 (PDF p. 5); the tables used are S6 Table A (rendered p. 1) and S6 Table C (rendered p. 2)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected text; Sol's smallest_repair, validated.json, P041-E006, verbatim] Replace the Study 3 exclusion and confinement language with: “In Study 3 we did not detect a statistically clear full-follow-up positive-versus-negative valence effect, and its relative-effect estimate is imprecise. Early absolute survival contrasts were smaller on the sampled former-senator pages, including in cited-only comparisons. These results do not establish absence of relative bias, identify political inactivity as a cause, or rule out cultural or policy-enforcement explanations.” Retain the abstract’s correct nondetection wording and the Discussion’s mechanism qualification.
[Mathematical content of the corrected claims] Notation (not in the paper). For a printed hazard ratio $h > 0$ with printed standard error $s > 0$ on the hazard-ratio scale, put $\sigma = s/h$ (the delta-method standard error of $\log h$) and $z(h,s) = \log(h)/\sigma = h\log(h)/s$. Printed values: former senators, $h_F = 0.691$, $s_F = 0.318$ (S6 Table C, first column); active senators, $h_A = 0.629$, $s_A = 0.091$ (S6 Table A, first column); $\sigma_F = s_F/h_F$, $\sigma_A = s_A/h_A$. Each printed value $v$ stands for a number in $[v - 0.0005,\ v + 0.0005]$, and the inequalities of (a) to (c) hold for every such choice of the four numbers.
(a) [‘did not detect’] $0.80 < |z(h_F, s_F)| < 0.81$; in particular $|z(h_F,s_F)| < 1$. At the printed values $z(h_F,s_F) = -0.80316\ldots$, whose two-sided normal p value is $0.42$, the pooled value printed on p. 5/8. The Study 3 hazard ratio is not distinguishable from 1 at any conventional level.
(b) [‘its relative-effect estimate is imprecise’] $|\log h_F - \log h_A| < 0.21\,\sigma_F < \tfrac{49}{25}\,\sigma_F$ and $|\log h_F| < \tfrac{49}{25}\,\sigma_F$. Hence the 95% Wald interval for the former-senator hazard ratio, $\exp(\log h_F \pm \tfrac{49}{25}\sigma_F)$, which is about $[0.280,\ 1.703]$ at the printed values (lower endpoint between $0.279$ and $0.282$, upper endpoint between $1.700$ and $1.706$ over the rounding intervals), contains both $1$ and the active-senator estimate $0.629$: Study 3 excludes neither the absence of a relative bias nor a relative bias as large as the one estimated for active senators.
(c) [No detected difference between the two relative effects] With the two samples treated as independent, $z_d = (\log h_F - \log h_A)\big/\sqrt{\sigma_F^2 + \sigma_A^2}$ satisfies $0.18 < z_d < 0.21$ ($0.19487\ldots$ at the printed values, two-sided normal p value $0.845$): the printed estimates do not distinguish the relative effect on former senators' pages from that on active senators' pages.
(d) [‘Early absolute survival contrasts were smaller on the sampled former-senator pages’; exact, from the deposited counts] Let $D_g(t)$ be the proportion of positive facts surviving beyond $t$ hours minus the proportion of negative facts surviving beyond $t$ hours in group $g$ (A: Studies 1, 2, 4, with 150 positive and 150 negative facts; F: Study 3, with 75 positive and 76 negative facts). Within 12 hours, 52 positive and 75 negative facts are removed in A and 3 positive and 1 negative in F, so $D_A(12) = 23/150$, $D_F(12) = 1/76 - 3/75 = -51/1900$ and $D_A(12) - D_F(12) = 1027/5700 > 0$. Within 7 days (168 hours), 82 positive and 101 negative facts are removed in A and 7 positive and 3 negative in F, so $D_A(168) = 19/150$, $D_F(168) = 3/76 - 7/75 = -307/5700$ and $D_A(168) - D_F(168) = 343/1900 > 0$.
(e) [‘These results do not establish absence of relative bias’] By P041-T1 there are removal laws for two populations with the same positive-to-negative hazard ratio $2/3 \ne 1$ and 12-hour absolute contrasts $16/125$ and $9801/1000000$; so neither nondetection in F nor a smaller absolute contrast in F implies a hazard ratio of 1 in F.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. The printed entries of S6 Table A and S6 Table C: quoted in P041-T1; the table conventions (hazard ratios with standard errors on the hazard-ratio scale): standing assumption (S5). The three p values of p. 5/8 (0.70, 0.47 and 0.42 pooled): quoted in P041-T1. The sentences being replaced are transcribed in P041-T11.
Not in the paper. (a) The Wald calculation from a printed pair: with $\beta = \log h$ the Cox coefficient and $s = h\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\beta)}$ the delta-method standard error of $h = e^\beta$, the statistic for $\beta = 0$ is $z = \beta/\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\beta)} = h\log(h)/s$, and the two-sided normal p value is $2\Phi(-|z|)$ (validator, P041-E006/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 3–4; the same reading as in P041-T8). (b) The multiplier $49/25 = 1.96$ stands for the normal 97.5% point $1.959964\ldots$; nothing depends on the difference. (c) The comparison in (c) is the validator's delta-method calculation ‘Using only the printed rounded values’ (derivation.md, section 4: $\hat d = 0.094008567$, $s_d = 0.482407534$, $z = 0.194873754$, $p = 0.845491782$); it assumes independent active and former samples. (d) The removal counts are from the deposited data, standing assumption (S6); $D_g(t)$ is the validator's notation (derivation.md, section 5) and equals the valence coefficient of the survival regressions of S11 (compare P041-T9).
canonical_claim.note: The corrected text is a weaker conclusion, not a theorem; its formal content is what the printed numbers and the exact counts do and do not show. Parts (a) to (c) use only the printed three-decimal entries; they involve a logarithm and are stated as inequalities with room for rounding (checked on a grid over the rounding intervals when this list was fixed: |z| between 0.8009 and 0.8055; |log h_F - log h_A|/sigma_F between 0.2005 and 0.2081; z_d between 0.1912 and 0.1986). The validators' refits from the deposited data give the same picture with more digits (former-senator hazard ratio 0.691383 with 95% interval [0.280851, 1.702006] after Stata's n/(n-1) factor; ratio of the former to the active hazard ratio 1.117767 with p = 0.8128 in a model with study indicators, and 1.093696 with p = 0.852 with study-specific baselines); those are Cox fits and are not targets. Part (d) is the exact part of the second sentence: the contrasts themselves. The between-population p values attached to them (0.0019 at 12 hours, 0.0038 at 7 days), and the cited-only comparisons, involve regression standard errors and normal tails and are not targets. The clauses about causes and mechanisms are interpretive and have no formal content beyond (e), which is a corollary of P041-T1 and should reuse its definitions. The second validator's wording of the repair (validated.json, second_validator.smallest_repair) has the same formal content.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Abstract, ‘Negative facts are 36% more likely to be removed by Wikipedia editors than positive facts within 12 hours and 29% more likely within 3 days’, and ‘Effects of Citations on Survival’, ‘uncited (but true) facts are 64% more likely to be removed than cited facts within four hours’, as printed; the counts are the validators' recounts of the deposited data and are not printed in the paper
canonical_claim.location: Abstract, p. 1/8 (PDF p. 1); ‘Effects of Citations on Survival’, sentence running from p. 4/8 to p. 5/8 (PDF pp. 4–5)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact refutation of the three printed percentages under their natural reading (the counts are recounts of the deposited data and are not printed in the paper).
Reading (Sol's natural reading, validated.json, P041-E001). ‘A is $x$% more likely to be removed than B within time $t$’ compares the proportions removed by time $t$, with B as the reference: $p_A = (1 + x/100)\,p_B$, that is, $x = R(p_A, p_B) := 100\,(p_A/p_B - 1)$, for $p_B > 0$. A printed whole number $k$ is the rounding of $x$ when $k - \tfrac12 \le x < k + \tfrac12$.
Counts. (1) Negative against positive facts, Studies 1, 2, 4, within 12 hours: 75 of 150 against 52 of 150 removed. (2) The same comparison within 72 hours: 92 of 150 against 69 of 150. (3) Uncited against cited facts, Studies 1 and 4, within 4 hours: 62 of 100 against 32 of 100.
Claims. (i) $R(75/150,\ 52/150) = 575/13 = 44.2307\ldots$; $R(92/150,\ 69/150) = 100/3 = 33.3333\ldots$; $R(62/100,\ 32/100) = 375/4 = 93.75$. (ii) None of these is rounded by the printed number: $575/13 - 36 = 107/13 > \tfrac12$, $100/3 - 29 = 13/3 > \tfrac12$ and $375/4 - 64 = 119/4 > \tfrac12$. So ‘36%’, ‘29%’ and ‘64%’ are false as relative increases in the proportion removed; the roundings of the three relative increases are 44, 33 and 94. (iii) The printed numbers are instead the roundings of the symmetric percentage difference of the two removal counts, $M(a,b) := 100\,|a - b|\big/\big((a+b)/2\big)$, which is the expression evaluated in lines 33, 38 and 43 of the deposited (Harvard) do-file: $M(75,52) = 4600/127 = 36.2204\ldots \in [35.5,\ 36.5)$, $M(92,69) = 200/7 = 28.5714\ldots \in [28.5,\ 29.5)$ and $M(62,32) = 3000/47 = 63.8297\ldots \in [63.5,\ 64.5)$. (iv) In general, for real numbers $a > b > 0$ (removal counts in two groups of the same size, so that $p_A/p_B = a/b$), with $R = 100\,(a/b - 1)$ and $M = 200\,(a-b)/(a+b)$: $$R - M = \frac{100\,(a-b)^2}{b\,(a+b)} > 0,$$ so the symmetric difference always understates the relative increase. For the three pairs $R - M = 13225/1651$, $100/21$ and $5625/188$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. The two sentences, quoted in full in P041-T12. The paper gives no formula for the three percentages and no table that contains them; ‘within 3 days’ is 72 hours.
From the deposited data and code (not in the paper). The rule for ‘removed by $h$ hours’ and the arm sizes: standing assumption (S6). The do-file's ‘Main findings’ block (Harvard do-file, lines 30–43) counts removals with ‘count if (treat_final==1 | treat_final==2) & round!=3 & round < 5 & dead==1 & hours_alive<=12’ and its analogues and then evaluates, at lines 33, 38 and 43, ‘disp ((abs(75 - 52)/((75 + 52)/2)) * 100)’, ‘disp ((abs(92 - 69)/((92 + 69)/2)) * 100)’ and ‘disp ((abs(62 - 32)/((62 + 32)/2)) * 100)’. The six counts (75, 52; 92, 69; 62, 32) and the group sizes (150 and 150; 100 and 100) were recounted from the staged CSV by both validators and again when this list was fixed.
Not in the paper: the names $R$ (relative increase in the proportion removed, reference group in the denominator) and $M$ (symmetric percentage difference); the rounding rule.
canonical_claim.note: Pure rational arithmetic. The finding was validated twice (both verdicts confirmed, evidence type exact_counterexample; the second validator's files are under P041-E001/v2/artifact/). It also touches headline claim P041-H3 (the 64% of the citation comparison), and the third comparison is the whole of the defect confirmed under P041-N006. What is refuted is the label: the wording ‘x% more likely … than’ applied to numbers computed as a difference over the mean of the two counts. The counts, the direction of the three comparisons and the hazard ratios 1.59 and 2.33 are not in question (‘No defect in the three removal counts, direction of the comparisons, or Cox model estimates is established’). Part (iv) is the validator's Step 4, stated there for proportions $p_A > p_B > 0$; with equal group sizes it is the same identity in the counts.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Abstract, the sentence with ‘36%’ and ‘29%’, and ‘Effects of Citations on Survival’, the sentence with ‘64%’, as repaired by Sol: 44%, 33% and 94%, computed as relative increases in the proportion removed
canonical_claim.location: Abstract, p. 1/8 (PDF p. 1); ‘Effects of Citations on Survival’, pp. 4/8–5/8 (PDF pp. 4–5)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected text; Sol's prior_correction.corrected_text, validated.json, P041-E001, verbatim] “With the deposited stored durations, negative facts have a 44.23% higher removal risk than positive facts within 12 hours and a 33.33% higher risk within 3 days; uncited facts have a 93.75% higher removal risk than cited facts within four hours. Calculate these directional increases as 100(p_comparison/p_reference-1). If a separate timestamp correction adopts the original minute strings with an inclusive 12-hour cutoff, the first increase would instead be 46.15%.”
[Sol's smallest_repair, verbatim] “Using the deposited stored durations, replace 36% with 44% and 29% with 33% in the abstract, and replace 64% with 94% in the citation paragraph. At two decimal places these are 44.23%, 33.33%, and 93.75%. Update the corresponding do-file calculations to use the reference risk as denominator. An alternative is to retain the existing numbers and explicitly describe symmetric percentage differences, which changes the reported measure.” With the first repair the two sentences read ‘Negative facts are 44% more likely to be removed by Wikipedia editors than positive facts within 12 hours and 33% more likely within 3 days’ and ‘uncited (but true) facts are 94% more likely to be removed than cited facts within four hours’.
[Mathematical content] With $R(p_A, p_B) = 100\,(p_A/p_B - 1)$, $M(a,b) = 100\,|a-b|\big/\big((a+b)/2\big)$ and the rounding rule of P041-T3:
(i) $R(75/150,\ 52/150) = 575/13$, with $43.5 \le 575/13 < 44.5$ and $|575/13 - 44.23| \le 0.005$.
(ii) $R(92/150,\ 69/150) = 100/3$, with $32.5 \le 100/3 < 33.5$ and $|100/3 - 33.33| \le 0.005$.
(iii) $R(62/100,\ 32/100) = 375/4 = 93.75$, with $93.5 \le 375/4 < 94.5$.
(iv) [The conditional variant] If the number of negative facts removed within 12 hours is 76 in place of 75 (the count obtained from the recorded minute-resolution time strings with an inclusive 12-hour cut-off; finding P041-E002), then $R(76/150,\ 52/150) = 600/13 = 46.1538\ldots$, with $45.5 \le 600/13 < 46.5$ and $|600/13 - 46.15| \le 0.005$.
(v) [The alternative repair] The printed 36, 29 and 64 are the roundings of $M(75,52) = 4600/127$, $M(92,69) = 200/7$ and $M(62,32) = 3000/47$; the printed numbers are therefore correct if described as percentage differences relative to the mean of the two removal counts, a different measure from the one the wording names.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
As for P041-T3: the counts (75 and 52 of 150 within 12 hours; 92 and 69 of 150 within 72 hours; 62 and 32 of 100 within 4 hours), the measures $R$ and $M$ and the rounding rule. The printed sentences being replaced are transcribed in P041-T12.
For (iv), not in the paper: the deposited durations are stored in single precision; rebuilding them from the recorded time strings changes one classification at the 12-hour horizon (a Study 1 negative, cited fact whose recorded strings are exactly 720 minutes apart and whose stored duration is 43,253,760 ms, more than 12 hours), giving 76 negative facts removed within 12 hours with the positive count 52 unchanged (validator, P041-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, Step 6; finding P041-E002).
canonical_claim.note: Also the corrected statement for the third comparison of headline claim P041-H3 and for P041-N006 (Minor), whose only established defect is that 64%. canonical_claim.statement:
Exact counterexample to the sufficiency of random order (validator's construction: a possible potential-outcome system, not a claim about the actual Wikipedia editors).
Setting. There are $2m$ pages, of which $m$ receive a cited fact (C) and $m$ an uncited fact (U). The order of insertion is a uniformly random permutation, independent of the assignment, so that the sequence of types $z = (z_1, \dots, z_{2m})$ at ranks $1, \dots, 2m$ is uniformly distributed over the $\binom{2m}{m}$ sequences with $m$ C's and $m$ U's. The outcome $Y_r \in \{0,1\}$ of the edit at rank $r$ is 1 if it is removed within a fixed duration after its insertion. Editor response: an uncited edit starts a period of heightened scrutiny of subsequent insertions from the account; an edit inserted during scrutiny is removed whatever its own citation status; an edit inserted outside scrutiny survives; nothing is removed retrospectively. Under the original, slow schedule consecutive insertions are far enough apart that scrutiny has expired before the next insertion, so $Y^{\mathrm{slow}}_r(z) = 0$ for all $r$ and $z$. Under the accelerated schedule every insertion after the first uncited one is made while scrutiny is active, so $$Y_r(z) = \mathbf{1}\{\exists\, s < r : z_s = \mathrm{U}\}.$$ Let $D(z) = \frac1m\sum_{r:\,z_r = \mathrm{C}} Y_r(z) - \frac1m\sum_{r:\,z_r = \mathrm{U}} Y_r(z)$ be the cited-minus-uncited difference in removal rates, and $D^{\mathrm{slow}}$ the same with $Y^{\mathrm{slow}}$.
Claims. (i) [No direct effect] $Y_r(z)$ depends only on $z_1, \dots, z_{r-1}$: for every rank $r$ and all $z, z' \in \{\mathrm{C},\mathrm{U}\}^{2m}$ (balanced or not) that agree at every rank $s < r$, $Y_r(z) = Y_r(z')$. In particular, changing an edit's own citation status with its rank and all other edits fixed never changes its outcome: every controlled direct effect of citation is 0. (ii) [Slow schedule] $D^{\mathrm{slow}}(z) = 0$ for every $z$. (iii) [One block of Study 1, $m = 2$] The six equally likely type sequences give (types at ranks 1–4; outcomes at ranks 1–4; cited mean; uncited mean; $D$): (UUCC; 0111; 1; 1/2; 1/2), (UCUC; 0111; 1; 1/2; 1/2), (UCCU; 0111; 1; 1/2; 1/2), (CUUC; 0011; 1/2; 1/2; 0), (CUCU; 0011; 1/2; 1/2; 0), (CCUU; 0001; 0; 1/2; −1/2). Hence $\mathrm{E}[D] = \tfrac16\big(\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac12 + 0 + 0 - \tfrac12\big) = \tfrac16 \ne 0$. (iv) [General $m \ge 1$] Let $K$ be the number of cited edits that precede the first uncited edit. Then $\Pr(K = k) = \binom{2m-k-1}{m-1}\big/\binom{2m}{m}$ for $k = 0, \dots, m$, and $\mathrm{E}[K] = m/(m+1)$. Exactly $m - K$ cited edits and exactly $m - 1$ uncited edits are removed, so the expected cited removal rate is $1 - \mathrm{E}[K]/m = m/(m+1)$, the uncited removal rate is $(m-1)/m$ in every order, and $$\mathrm{E}[D] = \frac{m}{m+1} - \frac{m-1}{m} = \frac{1}{m(m+1)} > 0.$$ (v) [The size of Study 1, $m = 50$] $\mathrm{E}[K] = 50/51$; the expected cited removal rate is $50/51$; the uncited removal rate is $49/50$; $\mathrm{E}[D] = 1/2550 \ne 0$.
Consequence. The order is uniformly random and independent of a balanced citation assignment, every direct effect of citation is zero, and the expected cited-minus-uncited contrast is 0 under the original schedule and $1/(m(m+1)) \ne 0$ under the accelerated one. So random assignment of the order does not by itself imply that speeding up the implementation ‘does not bias our results’: the expected contrast under the implemented protocol, the expected contrast under the planned protocol and the direct effect need not coincide.
Boundary checks from the same artifact, which delimit the counterexample. (vi) If the outcome at each rank is a fixed pattern that does not depend on any treatment, the expected contrast is 0: for $m = 2$ and outcomes $(0,0,1,1)$ at ranks 1 to 4, $\mathrm{E}[D] = 0$. (vii) If instead each of 4 ranks is independently C or U with probability $1/2$ (16 equally likely sequences) and the scrutiny rule is the same, the Horvitz–Thompson contrast $\tfrac14\sum_{r=1}^{4}\big(2\cdot\mathbf{1}\{z_r = \mathrm{C}\} - 2\cdot\mathbf{1}\{z_r = \mathrm{U}\}\big)\,Y_r(z)$ has expectation 0. The non-zero expectation in (iii) to (v) arises under the assignment of a fixed number of cited and uncited facts, as in a Study 1 block.

[Mathematical content] Setting and notation of P041-T5: $2m$ ranks, $m$ cited (C) and $m$ uncited (U) edits, the type sequence $z$ uniformly distributed over the $\binom{2m}{m}$ balanced sequences, and $D(z)$ the cited-minus-uncited difference in mean outcomes.
(a) [What random order does give; the first sentence] Suppose the outcome of the edit at rank $r$ depends only on its rank and on its own type: $Y_r(z) = g(r, z_r)$ for a function $g : \{1, \dots, 2m\} \times \{\mathrm{C}, \mathrm{U}\} \to \mathbb{R}$, with no dependence on the types of the other edits ($g$ may vary with rank in any way, for instance because the schedule is uneven). Then $$\mathrm{E}[D] = \frac{1}{2m}\sum_{r=1}^{2m}\big(g(r,\mathrm{C}) - g(r,\mathrm{U})\big),$$ the average over ranks of the direct effect of citation. In particular, if $g(r,\mathrm{C}) = g(r,\mathrm{U}) = c_r$ for every $r$ (a fixed calendar pattern $c$ that does not depend on treatment), then $\mathrm{E}[D] = 0$; the validator's instance is $m = 2$, $c = (0,0,1,1)$.

canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; S11, first paragraph] “As a final robustness check, we examined the ordinary least squares estimates on survival at 6, 12, and 24 hours as well as 7 days. These results, presented in Tables A and B estimate the likelihood that an edit was removed by that point in time. The OLS estimates consistently find that for active senators, positive and cited facts are less likely to have been removed while for retired and dead senators (Study 3) there is no difference.” Table titles: “Table A: OLS Estimates on Survival at 6 Hours and 12 Hours”; “Table B: OLS Estimates on Survival at 24 Hours and 7 Days”. Printed coefficients, in the order Positive (N 300, Studies 1,2,4) | Cited (N 200, Studies 1,4) | Positive (N 151, Studies 3): 6 hrs: 0.113** | 0.320*** | -0.027; 12 hrs: 0.153*** | 0.370*** | -0.027; 24 hrs: 0.147*** | 0.390*** | -0.027; 7 Days: 0.127*** | 0.230*** | -0.054.
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair, validated.json, P041-E010, verbatim] “Replace was removed by that point in time with survived beyond that point in time in S11's second sentence. The corrected sentence is: These results, presented in Tables A and B, estimate the likelihood that an edit survived beyond that point in time. To reproduce the printed tables with the staged Yale do-file, also initialize each of hour6, hour12, hour24, and day7 to 1 and set it to 0 when hours_alive is at or below its horizon, matching Harvard lines 147–154.”
[Mathematical content] For a horizon of $h$ hours let $S_i(h) = 1$ if fact $i$ is not removed within $h$ hours and $0$ otherwise, and $R_i(h) = 1 - S_i(h)$.
(i) [Complementing the outcome reverses every slope] Let $X$ be an $n \times k$ real matrix of full column rank whose first column is the vector of ones $\mathbf{1}$, let $S \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $R = \mathbf{1} - S$. Then the least-squares coefficient vectors satisfy $\hat\beta_R = e_1 - \hat\beta_S$ with $e_1 = (1, 0, \dots, 0)^\top$: the intercept becomes one minus the intercept and every other coefficient changes sign. The residuals satisfy $u_R = -u_S$, so $\sum_i u_i^2\,x_i x_i^\top$, the robust covariance $\frac{n}{n-k}(X^\top X)^{-1}\big(\sum_i u_i^2\,x_i x_i^\top\big)(X^\top X)^{-1}$ and the standard errors are the same for the two outcomes.
(ii) [The printed coefficients are survival slopes] Models: (P) $S(h)$ on an intercept, the indicator of a positive fact and the indicators of Study 2 and of Study 4, over the 300 facts of Studies 1, 2, 4 (50 positive and 50 negative in each study); (C) $S(h)$ on an intercept, the indicator of a cited fact and the indicator of Study 4, over the 200 facts of Studies 1 and 4 (50 cited and 50 uncited in each); (F) $S(h)$ on an intercept and the indicator of a positive fact, over the 151 facts of Study 3 (75 positive, 76 negative). In (P) and (C) the treatment is balanced within every study, so the treatment coefficient is the difference between the two arms in the pooled proportion surviving; in (F) it is the difference in proportions. Numbers surviving beyond $h$ (treated arm, comparison arm): (P), of 150 and 150: $h = 6$: 105, 88; $h = 12$: 98, 75; $h = 24$: 90, 68; $h = 168$: 68, 49. (C), of 100 and 100: $h = 6$: 67, 35; $h = 12$: 63, 26; $h = 24$: 58, 19; $h = 168$: 34, 11. (F), of 75 and 76: $h = 6, 12, 24$: 72, 75; $h = 168$: 68, 73. The treatment coefficients are therefore (P) $17/150$, $23/150$, $11/75$, $19/150$; (C) $8/25$, $37/100$, $39/100$, $23/100$; (F) $-51/1900$, $-51/1900$, $-51/1900$, $-307/5700$. Each is within $0.0005$ of the printed entry: $0.113$, $0.153$, $0.147$, $0.127$; $0.320$, $0.370$, $0.390$, $0.230$; $-0.027$, $-0.027$, $-0.027$, $-0.054$.
(iii) [They are not removal slopes] By (i), with the outcome ‘removed by that point in time’, $R(h)$, the same twelve regressions give the negatives of these twelve numbers, for example $-17/150$ (which rounds to $-0.113$) for positive facts at 6 hours. Each printed coefficient is non-zero and has the sign of the survival slope, so none of the twelve is the rounding of the removal slope. Read as effects on removal, the printed positive coefficients for active senators would also contradict the paragraph's third sentence (‘positive and cited facts are less likely to have been removed’).

canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] S9 Table A (‘Covariates as Moderators of Positive Edits from Cox Regressions’): “Positive X Length of Incumbency / Coefficient: 0.989 | 0.981 / Standard error: (0.019) | (0.017)” (columns: N 300, Studies 1,2,4 | N 400, Studies 1,2,4,5). S9 Table B (‘Covariates as Moderators of Cited Edits from Cox Regressions’): “Cited X Length of Incumbency / Coefficient: 1.056*** | 1.056*** / Standard error: (0.020) | (0.019)”. S10 (‘Covariates Predicting Length of Survival from Cox Regressions’): “Incumbency Length / Coefficient: 1.004 / Standard error: (0.008)” (N 400, Studies 1,2,4,5). Deposited codebook, p. 1: “lengthofincumbency: Year Senator was first elected.”
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair, validated.json, P041-E004, verbatim] “Relabel the S9 rows Positive X First-election year and Cited X First-election year and the S10 row First-election year; correct accompanying lists describing this same fitted covariate. Optionally specify that larger years indicate shorter tenure. If retaining tenure labels, use L=2014-Y and transform the year main effect, interactions, associated treatment main effects, baseline, and covariance matrix as derived in artifact/derivation.md.”
[Mathematical content] Let $Y$ be the year of first election (the fitted covariate), $C = 2014$, $L = C - Y$ the length of tenure in years, $T \in \{0,1\}$ a treatment indicator (positive, or cited) and $w$ the remainder of the linear predictor. The fitted Cox hazard is $h(t \mid T, Y, w) = h_0(t)\exp(bY + aT + gTY + w)$.
(i) [Reparameterization] For all real $a, b, g, C, L, T, w$: $b(C - L) + aT + gT(C - L) + w = Cb + (-b)L + (a + Cg)T + (-g)TL + w$. Hence, with $b_L = -b$, $a_L = a + Cg$, $g_L = -g$ and $h_{0,L}(t) = h_0(t)\,e^{Cb}$, $$h_{0,L}(t)\exp(b_L L + a_L T + g_L TL + w) = h_0(t)\exp(bY + aT + gTY + w)\quad\text{whenever } Y = C - L:$$ the same fitted hazards, written in terms of tenure.
(ii) [Direction] The treatment hazard ratio at tenure $L$ is $\exp(a_L + g_L L)$, and one more year of tenure multiplies it by $e^{g_L} = e^{-g} = 1/e^{g}$, the reciprocal of the printed interaction ratio $r = e^{g}$. In S10's model (no terms in $T$) one more year of tenure multiplies the hazard by $e^{-b} = 1/e^{b}$. So a printed ratio below 1 corresponds to a ratio per year of tenure above 1, and conversely: the printed S9 Table A entries ($0.989$, $0.981$) correspond to tenure ratios above 1, and the printed S9 Table B entries ($1.056$, $1.056$) and S10 entry ($1.004$) to tenure ratios below 1. Read under their printed labels, as ratios per year of incumbency, all five entries have the direction reversed.
(iii) [Magnitudes from the printed entries] For every $r$ in the rounding interval $[v - 0.0005,\ v + 0.0005]$ of a printed $v$: for $v = 0.989$, $1.0106 < 1/r < 1.0117$; for $v = 0.981$, $1.0188 < 1/r < 1.0199$; for $v = 1.056$, $0.9465 < 1/r < 0.9475$, so that $1/r$ rounds to $0.947$; for $v = 1.004$, $0.9955 < 1/r < 0.9966$.
(iv) [Standard errors and tests] If $s = r\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(g)}$ is the delta-method standard error of $r = e^{g}$, the delta-method standard error of $1/r = e^{-g}$ is $(1/r)\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(g)} = s/r^2$, and the Wald statistic for no moderation is unchanged, $(-g)^2/\operatorname{Var}(g) = g^2/\operatorname{Var}(g)$. The three stars of the S9 Table B row therefore stand, with the direction reversed.
(v) [The validator's exact instance] Take $r = 132/125 = 1.056$ and relative hazards $r^{\,T(Y - 2009)}$. At $Y = 2009$ ($L = 5$) the treatment hazard ratio is $1$; at $Y = 2008$ ($L = 6$) it is $125/132 < 1$. One more year of first election multiplies the treatment hazard ratio by $132/125 > 1$, one more year of tenure multiplies it by $125/132 < 1$, and the product of the two multipliers is 1.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: ‘Replication on Wikipedia Pages of Dead and Retired Senators’ (the whole paragraph), with the last sentence of the first paragraph of the Discussion and the last two sentences of the Abstract; as printed
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. ‘Replication on Wikipedia Pages of Dead and Retired Senators’ (p. 5/8): “Wikipedia has special guidelines for articles that are biographies of living persons that require a more conservative approach to avoid libel [34]. To ensure that this more conservative approach does not explain our finding of editorial bias, Study 3 conducted a replication on the Wikipedia pages of senators who have left office since 1990. Both among senators who have left office and are still living and those who have passed away, we find no differences in the rates in which positive and negative facts are removed ($p$ = 0.70 and 0.47, respectively and $p$ = 0.42, pooled). If anything, the positive facts were removed more quickly than the negative ones. This suggests that the editorial bias cannot be explained by Wikipedia’s culture in general or by policies concerning biographies of living persons in particular. Instead, our findings suggest the editorial bias is limited to active politicians, the types of people for whom the stakes of a positive public image are the highest.”
Discussion, first paragraph (p. 5/8): “This experiment demonstrated that a substantial editorial bias exists for the Wikipedia pages of current U.S. senators. Across four studies, we consistently find that negative facts are more likely to be removed and are removed more quickly than positive facts. In a test conducted on the Wikipedia pages of recently retired and deceased senators, we find no editorial bias, suggesting that this bias is limited to the pages of active politicians and is not systemic to Wikipedia.”
Abstract (p. 1/8): “We replicate this study on the Wikipedia pages of deceased as well as recently retired but living senators and find no evidence of an editorial bias in either. Our results demonstrate that crowd-sourced information is subject to an editorial bias that favors the politically active.”
Qualification the paper attaches (Discussion, second paragraph, p. 5/8): “The reasons for the editorial bias toward positivity are not necessarily nefarious. It is plausible that Wikipedia editors are simply more conservative in applying their guidelines for living persons to active U.S. Senators than recently retired U.S. senators, even if the editing policies are nominally identical for both types of articles.”
Formalizable content of the passage, in the notation of P041-T2 and P041-T8 ($z(h,s) = h\log(h)/s$, $p = 2\,\Phi(-|z|)$). (P1) [The three p values] The printed pairs of S6 Table C, $(0.691,\ 0.318)$ pooled, $(0.775,\ 0.503)$ living and $(0.627,\ 0.406)$ deceased, give $|z| = 0.8032$, $0.3927$ and $0.7209$ and $p = 0.4219$, $0.6945$ and $0.4710$; over the rounding intervals of the printed pairs $p$ lies in $[0.4205,\ 0.4232]$, $[0.6936,\ 0.6954]$ and $[0.4700,\ 0.4720]$. These agree with the printed 0.42 (pooled), 0.70 (living) and 0.47 (deceased) to the precision the table entries allow, and in each case $|z| < 1$: none of the three comparisons is significant. This part of the passage is correct. (P2) [The inference] ‘we find no differences … This suggests that the editorial bias cannot be explained by … Instead, our findings suggest the editorial bias is limited to active politicians’ and ‘we find no editorial bias, suggesting that this bias is limited to the pages of active politicians and is not systemic to Wikipedia’ are read, for the purpose of the counterexample, as the implication: if the positive-against-negative comparison is statistically clear on active senators' pages and is not detected on former senators' pages, where the absolute contrast is also smaller, then the relative bias is absent on former senators' pages. P041-T1 refutes this implication, and P041-T2 (a) to (c) show that the printed estimates do not distinguish the hazard ratio on former senators' pages either from 1 or from the hazard ratio on active senators' pages.

canonical_claim.statement:

Although citations substantially increase an edit’s survival time, the editorial bias toward positivity is not eliminated by inclusion of a citation.”
‘Effects of Citations on Survival’ (pp. 4/8–5/8): “Overall, we find large and statistically significant differences in the survival time of cited and uncited facts. Consistent with Wikipedia’s policy, uncited (but true) facts are 64% more likely to be removed than cited facts within four hours (hazard ratio = 2.33, $p<0.001$).”

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: S1 File, ‘Description of implementation’, last paragraph, and S5 File, ‘Description of implementation’, last four sentences; as printed
canonical_claim.location: S1 File (rendered p. 2); S5 File (rendered p. 2); the main article refers to these changes on p. 3/8 (PDF p. 3)
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. S1 File, last paragraph: “Because other Wikipedia editors became suspicious of this account’s uncited edits and threatened to block the account, we sped up the implementation and finished implementing the experiment sooner than anticipated, on 15 July 2014. Because the order in which edits were made was randomly assigned, this does not bias our results.”
S5 File, end of ‘Description of implementation’: “After implementing the first 50 edits on 6 November 2014, other Wikipedia editors became suspicious. We decided to convert all of the uncited edits in the remaining 50 edits to cited edits. Thus the first 50 edits had all four conditions while the last 50 edits only had positive or negative conditions, with all facts cited. Because the order in which edits were made was randomly assigned, this does not bias our results.”
Main article (p. 3/8): “In S5 File, we report one concluding study to replicate Studies 1 and 4 that was partially aborted due to problems in the implementation, the inclusion of which does not change the results.” and “In order to prevent confounding, the order in which the edits were made, the time of day, the name of the editing Wikipedia account, and the IP address used to make the edit were randomly assigned as well.”
Formalizable content. The sentence ‘Because the order in which edits were made was randomly assigned, this does not bias our results’ gives the random assignment of the order as a sufficient reason for the conclusion. It is read, for the purpose of the counterexample, as the implication: whenever the order of the edits is uniformly random and independent of the treatment assignment, a change of schedule made in response to editors' reactions to earlier edits leaves the expected treatment contrast equal to its value under the planned schedule and to the direct effect of the treatment. P041-T5 refutes this implication (zero direct effect, expected contrast 0 under the planned schedule and $1/(m(m+1))$ under the accelerated one), and P041-T6 (a) gives a condition under which the expected contrast does equal the average direct effect: no edit's outcome depends on the treatments of other edits.

From the paper: the design and the random assignment of the order, standing assumptions (S2), (S3); S1 File (rendered p. 1): “From 7-15 July 2014, we inserted randomly assigned facts into the Wikipedia pages of U.S. senators. The time, order, Wikipedia account, valence (positive or negative), and citation (or not) were all randomly assigned.”; S5 File (rendered p. 1): “Senators who received a positive fact in Study 4 received a negative fact here and vice-versa. The citation (cited or not) was randomly assigned independent of valence.
